course.title: Negotiation & Persuasion
course.description: A practical introduction to principled negotiation — separating people from problems, trading on interests, and reaching agreements you can defend. Built from openly-licensed OER Commons material on Negotiation & Conflict Resolution (CC BY), drawing on the Fisher, Ury & Patton framework.

questions.prompt: In principled negotiation, you should focus primarily on…
questions.explanation: Fisher & Ury's core move: focus on interests, not positions — see 'Interests, not positions'.

questions.prompt: BATNA stands for…
options: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement
questions.explanation: Your BATNA is what you'll do if there's no deal — see 'BATNA & the ZOPA'.

questions.prompt: The ZOPA (zone of possible agreement) exists when…
options: the seller's minimum is above the buyer's maximum
the buyer's maximum is above the seller's minimum
both sides make the same opening offer
questions.explanation: A deal is possible only when the ranges overlap — see 'BATNA & the ZOPA'.

questions.prompt: An 'anchor' in negotiation is…
options: the first number that shapes the range
questions.explanation: The first offer pulls expectations toward it — see 'Preparation & anchoring'.

questions.prompt: 'Claiming value' refers to…
options: expanding the pie so both gain
dividing the existing pie between the parties
questions.explanation: Claiming = dividing; creating = expanding — see 'Creating vs claiming value'.

questions.prompt: Which move tends to CREATE value?
options: trading across issues you value differently
questions.explanation: Trades on differing priorities enlarge the pie — see 'Creating vs claiming value'.

questions.prompt: A good response to a 'take it or leave it' ultimatum is to…
options: name the tactic and redirect to criteria
questions.explanation: Naming a hardball tactic defuses it — see 'Hardball tactics & difficult conversations'.

questions.prompt: Grounding a disagreement in 'objective criteria' means using…
options: fair, independent standards both sides accept
questions.explanation: Objective standards (market rate, precedent) keep it principled — see 'Interests, not positions'.

lessons.title: Interests, not positions
lessons.grammar_note: Position = what you say you want. Interest = why you want it. Ask 'why' to move from one to the other.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell a *position* from an *interest* and reframe a standoff around interests. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which should you focus on — the demand, or the reason behind it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Principled negotiation (Fisher, Ury & Patton, *Getting to Yes*) rests on four moves: separate the people from the problem, focus on *interests* not *positions*, invent options for mutual gain, and insist on *objective criteria*. A position is the concrete thing you demand ('I want $60,000'); an interest is the underlying need it serves (security, recognition, a fair rate). Positions collide; interests often overlap, because many different positions can satisfy the same interest.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Two people quarrel over one orange, each demanding the whole thing (positions). Asked *why*, one wants the peel to bake, the other the fruit to eat (interests). Splitting by interest gives each 100% of what they need — a result impossible while they argue over positions. That single 'why?' turned a fight into a trade.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For each, name the likely interest behind the position: (1) an employee demands a corner office; (2) a client insists on a 20% discount; (3) a neighbor demands the fence be moved one metre; (4) a teammate insists on being sole author. Answers: (1) status/quiet to focus; (2) budget certainty or feeling they got a fair deal; (3) privacy or sunlight; (4) recognition for their contribution.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the first number as the real goal — it's usually a proxy for an interest. Mistake: attacking the person instead of the problem. Exit: (a) Turn this position into a question that surfaces an interest: 'I won't go below $5,000.' (b) Name the standard you'd cite to keep it objective. Answers: (a) 'What does the $5,000 need to cover for you?'; (b) an independent benchmark such as market rate, an appraisal, or precedent.

lessons.title: BATNA & the ZOPA
lessons.grammar_note: Your BATNA is your walk-away power. The ZOPA is where a deal can live — only when the two acceptable ranges overlap.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define your *BATNA*, set a *reservation value*, and decide whether a *ZOPA* exists. Warm-up: what will you actually do if this negotiation fails?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Your *BATNA* — Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — is your best course of action with no deal. It sets your *reservation value*: the least favourable terms you'd still accept, because anything worse loses to simply walking away. The *ZOPA* (Zone Of Possible Agreement) is the overlap between your reservation value and the other side's. If the buyer will pay up to $100 and the seller will accept as little as $80, the ZOPA is $80–$100; if the seller's floor is $110, there is *no* ZOPA and no deal makes both better off. Improve your BATNA before you talk and your reservation value — and your confidence — improve with it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: You're offered a job at $70k. Your BATNA is a standing offer elsewhere at $72k, so your reservation value is about $72k — below that, you walk. If this employer can go up to $80k, the ZOPA is roughly $72k–$80k, and any figure inside it beats your alternative. Knowing this, you negotiate from strength instead of gratitude.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) Buyer's max is $15k, seller's min is $12k — is there a ZOPA, and what is it? (2) Buyer's max is $9k, seller's min is $11k — ZOPA? (3) Your only alternative just fell through — does your BATNA get stronger or weaker? (4) You line up a second supplier — stronger or weaker BATNA? Answers: (1) yes, $12k–$15k; (2) none — no deal beats both alternatives; (3) weaker; (4) stronger.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing your BATNA (an action you can take alone) with your reservation value (a number). Mistake: bluffing a strong BATNA you don't have — it collapses when tested. Exit: (a) If your BATNA improves, which way does your reservation value move? (b) Can a deal be reached with no ZOPA? Answers: (a) it becomes more demanding in your favour; (b) no — you must create value or walk.

lessons.title: Preparation & anchoring
lessons.grammar_note: Anchoring: the first number reframes the whole range. Prepare one — and justify it — so you're not the one being anchored.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Prepare a negotiation systematically and use — or resist — an *anchor*. Warm-up: why does the very first number on the table matter so much?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Most negotiations are won before anyone speaks. Preparation means listing your interests and theirs, knowing your BATNA and estimating theirs, gathering *objective criteria*, and setting three numbers: your target, your first offer, and your reservation value. *Anchoring* is the cognitive pull of the first figure named — subsequent discussion drifts toward it. A well-prepared, well-justified opening anchor shapes the range in your favour; when the other side anchors first, you resist by questioning its basis and re-anchoring with your own standard rather than haggling from theirs.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Selling a used car worth about $8,000, you open at $9,200 with a reason ('low mileage, new tyres, recent service'). The buyer now negotiates *down from* $9,200, and you likely settle near $8,300. Had you opened at $8,000, the buyer would have pushed you below it. The anchor — backed by a reason — did quiet work. Note the ethics: the anchor is ambitious but honestly justified, not a lie about the car.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) You know the market rate is $50–$55/hr; where do you open? (2) The other side opens with an extreme, unjustified number — accept it as the anchor, or challenge it? (3) Name two things to research before the table. (4) Which three numbers should you set in advance? Answers: (1) at or slightly above the top with a reason, e.g. $57 justified by your record; (2) challenge and re-anchor to a standard; (3) their interests and their likely BATNA (also market criteria); (4) first offer, target, reservation value.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: letting the other side anchor and then arguing only within their range. Mistake: opening with no justification, so your anchor is easy to dismiss. Exit: (a) What makes an anchor stick? (b) You're anchored by an extreme offer — what's your first response? Answers: (a) a credible reason tied to objective criteria; (b) question its basis and re-anchor to a fair standard, not a counter-extreme.

questions.prompt: The four elements of principled negotiation include all EXCEPT…
questions.explanation: Winning every concession is positional bargaining, not the principled method.

questions.prompt: Your reservation value is set by your…
questions.explanation: The strength of your best alternative defines the worst deal you'd accept.

questions.prompt: There is NO zone of possible agreement when…
questions.explanation: No overlap between acceptable ranges means no mutually beneficial deal.

questions.prompt: A first offer works as an anchor because it…
options: pulls the rest of the discussion toward it
questions.explanation: Anchoring biases later figures toward the first one named.

questions.prompt: The best way to strengthen your position before talks is to…
questions.explanation: A stronger alternative raises your reservation value and your confidence.

questions.prompt: Reframing 'I want the whole budget' as 'I need cost certainty' is a shift from…
questions.explanation: Naming the underlying need moves from position to interest.

lessons.title: Creating vs claiming value
lessons.grammar_note: Creating value = grow the pie (trade across differing priorities). Claiming value = divide the pie. Skilled negotiators do both, in that order.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish *creating* value from *claiming* it, and use trades to enlarge the deal. Warm-up: is negotiation always win–lose, or can both sides end up better off?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Every negotiation has two games. *Claiming value* is distributive — splitting a fixed pie, where your gain is my loss. *Creating value* is integrative — enlarging the pie before you split it. You create value by trading across issues the two sides *value differently*: I concede on what matters little to me but much to you, and vice versa. This is why 'interests, not positions' pays off — differences in priorities, forecasts, and risk tolerance are the raw material for mutual gain. The tension: to create value you must share information, yet to claim it you may want to hold information back. Handle the tension by expanding the pie first, then dividing it against objective criteria.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A supplier and a retailer argue over price alone (pure claiming). Adding issues, they discover the retailer values fast delivery and the supplier values a longer contract. They trade: guaranteed 12-month volume (cheap for the retailer to give, valuable to the supplier) in exchange for expedited shipping (cheap for the supplier, valuable to the retailer). Both leave better off than a price-only split would have allowed — value created, then the remaining margin claimed on fair terms.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) Is dividing a fixed sum creating or claiming? (2) You care about start date; they care about scope — how might you trade? (3) Name one thing that lets two sides 'grow the pie'. (4) Why can revealing an interest sometimes help you? Answers: (1) claiming; (2) flex the date they don't mind in exchange for scope you don't mind — trade low-cost gives for high-value gets; (3) issues valued differently by each side; (4) it lets the other side offer something cheap to them but valuable to you.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating every negotiation as a fixed pie (the 'mythical fixed pie' bias). Mistake: haggling one issue at a time, which hides the trades. Exit: (a) What must you often share to create value? (b) Which comes first, expanding or dividing? Answers: (a) information about your interests and priorities; (b) expand, then divide against objective criteria.

lessons.title: Hardball tactics & difficult conversations
lessons.grammar_note: Name the tactic to neutralise it. In tough conversations, separate the person from the problem — be soft on people, hard on the issue.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognise common hardball tactics and steer a heated exchange back to the problem. Warm-up: what could you say when someone gives you a flat 'take it or leave it'?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Hardball tactics try to pressure you off a fair process: extreme *anchors*, the ultimatum ('take it or leave it'), good-cop/bad-cop, false deadlines, and the *nibble* (a small extra ask after you thought you were done). The reliable counter is to *name the tactic* — 'That sounds like a take-it-or-leave-it; can we look at what a fair rate would be?' — which pulls the conversation back to interests and objective criteria. In difficult conversations, use active listening and 'I' statements, separate the people from the problem (be soft on the person, firm on the issue), and remember Ury's move: *go to the balcony* — pause and observe rather than react, so emotion doesn't hand control to the other side.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Mini-case: mid-deal, the buyer says 'This is my final number, decide now.' You go to the balcony (a breath, not a reaction) and reply: 'I hear that this is where you'd like to land. So I understand it — what standard puts the figure there? If it's the market rate, let's use the same rate for the whole deal.' The ultimatum is named, reframed around criteria, and the pressure quietly dissolves — without a counter-threat.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) After you agree, they add 'and you'll cover shipping too' — which tactic, and what do you do? (2) They set a deadline of 'end of day, no exceptions' — reasonable to test it? (3) An 'I' statement version of 'You're being unfair'? (4) What does 'go to the balcony' mean? Answers: (1) the nibble — reopen the whole package or decline the add-on; (2) yes, most deadlines are softer than stated; (3) 'I don't yet see how this figure is fair to me — can we check it against a standard?'; (4) pause and observe rather than react in the moment.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: meeting a hardball tactic with your own, which escalates and wrecks the relationship. Mistake: taking an attack personally instead of redirecting to the problem. Exit: (a) What's the first step against a named tactic? (b) 'Soft on the ___, hard on the ___.' Answers: (a) name it aloud and reframe around objective criteria; (b) soft on the person, hard on the problem.

items.translation: the specific thing a party demands in a negotiation
items.example: 'I won't pay more than $50' is a position, not an interest.

items.translation: the underlying need or motivation behind a position
items.example: Behind the low price was an interest in staying on budget.

items.translation: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — what you'll do if no deal is reached
items.example: A strong BATNA let her walk away from a bad offer.

items.translation: the least favourable terms you'd still accept, set by your BATNA
items.example: Below his reservation value, no deal beat walking away.

items.translation: Zone Of Possible Agreement — the overlap between both sides' acceptable ranges
items.example: With the seller's floor above the buyer's ceiling, there was no ZOPA.

items.translation: the pull of the first number named, which shapes the whole range
items.example: Her justified opening anchor set the tone for the deal.

questions.prompt: Trading two issues the sides value differently is an example of…
questions.explanation: Trades across differing priorities enlarge the pie — integrative bargaining.

questions.prompt: The 'mythical fixed pie' bias is the belief that…
options: the total value can't be enlarged
questions.explanation: It wrongly assumes negotiation is purely distributive.

questions.prompt: The 'nibble' is a tactic where the other side…
options: adds a small extra demand after apparent agreement
questions.explanation: A last-minute add-on once you think you're done.

questions.prompt: Naming a hardball tactic out loud tends to…
options: neutralise it and refocus on criteria
questions.explanation: Naming it moves the talk back to a fair process.

questions.prompt: 'Go to the balcony' means…
options: pause and observe instead of reacting
questions.explanation: Ury's phrase for stepping back from emotional reaction.

questions.prompt: 'Be soft on the ___, hard on the ___.'
questions.explanation: Separate the people from the problem — firm on the issue, respectful of the person.

lessons.title: Applied project: prepare for a real negotiation

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose a real negotiation you could plausibly have in the next month — a raise, a rent renewal, a project scope, a purchase — and build a one-page preparation plan using the tools from this course. You won't run it here; you'll plan it rigorously enough to walk in ready.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) INTERESTS: list your top three interests and your best guess at the other side's three (remember: why, not just what). 2) BATNA: state your Best Alternative and the reservation value it sets — then note one concrete way you could strengthen that BATNA first. 3) OPENING: write a specific opening offer or anchor and the objective criterion (market rate, precedent, appraisal) that justifies it. 4) CONCESSIONS: list two trades where you'd give something cheap to you but valuable to them, in exchange for something valuable to you — plus one hardball tactic you might face and your response.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Interests are needs, not positions (no bare numbers). ✔ Your BATNA is a real action, and the reservation value follows from it. ✔ Your opening is ambitious but honestly justified by a standard — not a bluff or a lie. ✔ Your concessions are genuine trades across differing priorities, not just splitting the difference. ✔ You named a likely tactic and a principled, non-escalating response. If all five hold, you've prepared like a principled negotiator.
